Let \(m=2q^2\), so \(n=2m\).  The answer is

\[
\boxed{\,r(r-1)\,\ell^{r-3}(\ell+1-r)\frac{\ell^{r-2}-1}{\ell-1}\, } .
\]

Here is the derivation.

For \(\sigma\in \Gamma\) with \(\pi_\sigma=\pi\), write

\[
\sigma(\alpha_i^{(j)})=\zeta^{a_i^{(j)}}\alpha_{\pi(i)}^{(j)},\qquad
\sigma(\rho_j)=\zeta^{s_j}\rho_j .
\]

The relation \(\prod_i\alpha_i^{(j)}=\rho_{j+1}\) gives

\[
\sum_i a_i^{(j)}=s_{j+1}.
\]

Pair the \(n=4q^2\) indices into the \(m=2q^2\) transpositions of \(\pi\).  For a transposition \(T=\{i,\pi(i)\}\), put

\[
x_T^{(j)}=a_i^{(j)}+a_{\pi(i)}^{(j)}.
\]

Then

\[
\sum_T x_T^{(j)}=s_{j+1}.
\]

On \(\Omega_k\), after applying \(\sigma^2\), the \(u\)-coordinate is translated by

\[
2k_js_j+x_T^{(j)}-x_{T'}^{(j)}.
\]

Thus the number of \(2\)-cycles depends only on the multiset \(\{x_T\}_{T}\subset \mathbb F_\ell^r\).  Conjugation by the lifted centralizer of \(\pi\) permutes the transpositions and does not change \(s\), so the conjugacy orbit is determined by \(s\) together with that multiset.

The imposed three-level cycle-count condition is equivalent, via finite Fourier transform on \(\mathbb F_\ell^r\), to the autocorrelation spectrum

\[
|\widehat a(\chi)|=
\begin{cases}
q+4Q,& \chi\in U^\perp\setminus\{1\},\\
q+2Q,& \chi\in W^\perp\setminus U^\perp,\\
q,& \chi\notin W^\perp,
\end{cases}
\]

where \(a(x)\) is the multiplicity of \(x\) among the \(x_T\).  Because \(q,q+2Q,q+4Q\equiv 2^{-1}\pmod \ell\) and \(2\) generates \(\mathbb F_\ell^\times\), these primes are inert in the \(\ell\)-cyclotomic character field.  Hence each Fourier coefficient is forced, up to a common translate, and the moment condition

\[
\sum_T x_T=Ps
\]

fixes that translate uniquely.  Therefore, for each admissible triple \((s,W,U)\), there is exactly one \(\widetilde C_\pi\)-conjugacy orbit.

It remains to count admissible \(s\) and flags.

The condition

\[
\mathbf 1\in \operatorname{span}\{s,Ps\}
\]

means there exist \(A,B\in\mathbb F_\ell\), not both zero, such that

\[
A s_j+B s_{j+1}=1
\]

for all \(j\).  The nonconstant solutions are exactly

\[
s_j=1+\mu\lambda^{j-1},
\]

where \(\lambda\) has order \(r\) and \(\mu^r=1\).  The conditions \(\sum_j s_j=r\) and \(\prod_j s_j=2\) force precisely this form, and all entries are nonzero.  There are

\[
r(r-1)
\]

such vectors \(s\).

For such an \(s\),

\[
c_s^{(t)}=\left(\frac{s_{1+t}}{s_1},\ldots,\frac{s_{r+t}}{s_r}\right)
\]

lies in a fixed \(2\)-dimensional subspace \(C\), and the \(r\) projective directions \(c_s^{(t)}\) are distinct.  A hyperplane \(U\) containing \(C\) can be chosen in

\[
\frac{\ell^{r-2}-1}{\ell-1}
\]

ways.  For each such \(U\), the number of codimension-\(2\) subspaces \(W\subset U\) avoiding all \(r\) directions \(c_s^{(t)}\) is

\[
\ell^{r-3}(\ell+1-r).
\]

Multiplying gives

\[
r(r-1)\cdot \frac{\ell^{r-2}-1}{\ell-1}\cdot \ell^{r-3}(\ell+1-r).
\]

So the required number is

\[
\boxed{\,r(r-1)\,\ell^{r-3}(\ell+1-r)\frac{\ell^{r-2}-1}{\ell-1}\, } .
\]
